Django was first released in July 2005, from a repository that had until then belonged to World Online, the web department of a newspaper in Lawrence, Kansas, where it was built (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`, `docs/faq/general.txt`; [Where Django came from, and who makes it](introduction/origins.md)).

Since then a release numbered A.B has been a **feature release**, and one numbered A.B.C a **patch release** of its series, issued to fix bugs and security issues (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).

DEP 4, written that year, set out that schedule; a **Django Enhancement Proposal**, a DEP, is the design document in which the project proposes a major change and records the decision (`deps:final/0004-release-schedule.rst`; [Where Django came from, and who makes it](introduction/origins.md#django-enhancement-proposals)).

Some feature releases are **long-term support releases**, given security and data-loss fixes for at least three years: 1.4 was the first, then 1.8 and 1.11 (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`, `docs/releases/1.11.txt`), and from 2.0, as DEP 4 laid down, a series runs X.0, X.1 and X.2, the last its long-term release.

Some feature releases are **long-term support releases**, given security and data-loss fixes for at least three years: 1.4 was the first, then 1.8 and 1.11 (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`, `docs/releases/1.11.txt`), and from 2.0, as DEP 4 laid down, a series runs X.0, X.1 and X.2, the last its long-term release.

From January 2028 Django makes one feature release a year, numbered by its year, each supported for three years: in its first year with the fixes the newest release receives now, in its next two with security and data-loss fixes alone, so that every release has what only the long-term ones had (`deps:accepted/0020-annual-release-cycle.rst`).
The releases that were to be 7.0 and 7.1 are Django 2028 and Django 2029 (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`; [Django's version: `VersionTuple` and `get_version`](utils/version.md)).

This commit is main on 26 September 2026, a pre-alpha of 6.2, which `django.VERSION` writes as an alpha of iteration 0, `(6, 2, 0, "alpha", 0)` (`django/utils/version.py:get_version`); 6.1.1 is the newest release, and 6.2 is expected in April 2027.

The figure sets the releases in their years, from their notes and, for 0.90, 0.96 and 1.0, the project's announcements (`docs/releases/`): look for the long-term releases, the change of rhythm at 1.8 and again in 2028, and where this commit stands.

A fix for a critical bug in the newest feature release goes to that release's branch as well as to main; a fix for a security issue or for the loss of data goes to main, to the last two feature releases and to any long-term release still supported (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).

Since 6.1 that is one of three **fetch modes**, `FETCH_ONE`, beside `FETCH_PEERS`, which fetches it at once for other instances the same run of the queryset made, and `FETCH_RAISE`, which refuses (`django/db/models/fetch_modes.py`; [What changed in querysets](changes/querysets.md)).

**Safer defaults**: aware datetimes (5.0), 64-bit automatic keys (6.0), `"https"` as the scheme a form's URL field assumes (6.0; `django/forms/fields.py:URLField`), and an iteration count for the PBKDF2 password hasher raised in every feature release, from 720,000 in 5.0 to 1,800,000 at this commit (`django/contrib/auth/hashers.py:PBKDF2PasswordHasher`).

It can change a behaviour outright: its notes list each such change as backwards incompatible, and the release process allows one where a path through deprecation is not possible or not worth its cost (`docs/internals/release-process.txt`).

The warning classes are named for the release that ends what they mark: `RemovedInDjango2028Warning` is a `DeprecationWarning` and `RemovedInDjango2029Warning` a `PendingDeprecationWarning`, and they were RemovedInDjango70Warning and RemovedInDjango71Warning until 6.2 renamed them for the calendar versions (`docs/releases/6.2.txt`).

To keep an old use working, the code has to recognise it: an old import of `MiddlewareMixin`, by its old module's `__getattr__` (`django/utils/deprecation.py:__getattr__`); an argument in its old position, through `deprecate_posargs` (`django/utils/deprecation.py:deprecate_posargs`); a model's own `from_db` written before 6.1 gave it a fetch mode, by inspecting its signature (`django/db/models/query.py:_get_from_db`); a field class that defines the old hook get_placeholder, as the class is made (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__init_subclass__`).

Some deprecations need a **transitional setting**, which lets a project take the new behaviour early or keep the old one for a time, and goes with the deprecation it serves: at this commit `URLIZE_ASSUME_HTTPS` (6.0), `USE_BLANK_CHOICE_DASH` (6.1) and `SIGNED_COOKIE_LEGACY_SALT_FALLBACK`, which came with a security fix in 5.2.15 and 6.0.6, each told in the section of its part (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

`USE_BLANK_CHOICE_DASH` and `SIGNED_COOKIE_LEGACY_SALT_FALLBACK`, which keep an old behaviour, warn when they are set, and `URLIZE_ASSUME_HTTPS`, which takes the new behaviour early, does not (`django/conf/__init__.py:Settings.__init__`; [What changed in settings, startup and the commands](changes/startup-and-commands.md)).

6.0 changed the setting's default from `AutoField` to `BigAutoField`, and nothing warns (`django/conf/global_settings.py`):

A project upgraded to 6.0 that never named the class finds the keys of its existing models changed under them, and makemigrations writes an `AlterField` to `BigAutoField` for each (`django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields`).

The 6.0 notes expected few projects to meet it: from 3.2 new projects had named `BigAutoField` themselves ([The second decade: from 1.9 to 5.0](changes/second-decade.md)), and a system check had warned those that named nothing (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`).
